title: A request is matched once, and the route table completes without crossing into dispatch
scope:
where the match happens and who may read it; telling a missing path from a refused verb;
binding a query parameter; an absent trailing segment; the closed set a capture may narrow to; building
an absolute link; reading the mount a request arrived through; which layer enforces `#[Access]`; and the
correction that routing is not a forcing case for typed `callable`. **Not in scope:** dispatch, a
controller convention, middleware and a return-value-to-response rule, all of which
[0077](0077.md) § 4 refuses and this ADR upholds; the framework layer that does
build them ([0082](0082.md) § 3); what an access *name* means
([0096](0096.md) § 2); the mount table's own
grammar ([0097](0097.md) § 3); and typed `callable` itself, which
§ 9 hands back to [0007](0007.md) § 3 with a corrected count.

summary.headline: A request is matched to its route once, before any of your code runs
summary.body:
The server matches an incoming request against the route table exactly once, before the handler,
and the result travels on the request, where `Core\Request::route()` returns it. The CSRF check,
the metrics label and the access decision all read that one answer. Around it, the table gained
what an application misses early: a wrong verb answers 405 rather than 404, a query parameter is
declared like a path capture, a trailing segment may be optional, a capture can narrow to a
closed set of typed values but never a regex, and links can be built absolute.
